title: Air Pollution in England: Ministers face the Environmental Audit Committee
label: 14 September 2026 · Air pollution evidence
summary: The Environmental Audit Committee questioned DEFRA and DFT ministers and officials about cross-government coordination, Ella's law, nitrogen and ammonia policy, air quality alerts, non-exhaust vehicle emissions, maritime and aviation pollution, traffic reduction measures, and the electric vehicle transition. The hearing revealed gaps in cross-departmental working, disagreements over the presentation of air quality data and ammonia regulation, and continued debate over how far central government should support local clean air schemes.

chapters.title: Cross-government working
chapters.takeaway: DEFRA admits coordination on air pollution could be better and is setting up a formal cross-government group.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Minister Hardy, how well are the Government working across departments on air pollution, and can you explain the contradictions you face?

turns.speaker: Emma Hardy
turns.text: I want to acknowledge the campaigners, especially Rosamund. On cross-government working, it could be better. We're launching a call for evidence this year as part of the air strategy due in 2028. I want to set up a formal cross-government group to openly discuss trade-offs, especially since there's been a change in Prime Minister.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We welcome that. I said to the previous panel we're disappointed MHCLG didn't send a minister. Is MHCLG recognising its role?

turns.speaker: Emma Hardy
turns.text: We haven't had a formal minister-to-minister conversation, but officials meet. We're trying to work in themes like healthy schools, which involve DfT, DfE and MHCLG. The worst government is when we're too siloed. It's work in progress.

chapters.title: Ella's law and legal limits
chapters.takeaway: Ministers say they support Ella's law's aims but are focusing on continuous improvement and better measurement rather than new legislation.

turns.speaker: Julia Buckley
turns.text: What consideration has been given to Ella's law's core principles in future legislation, and what barriers have you identified?

turns.speaker: Emma Hardy
turns.text: I fully support the ambition. I want to focus on what's most effective. Some targets focus on old pollutants like soot rather than modern ones. Also, once an area complies, it's like box ticked. I want a culture of continuous improvement, not static targets.

turns.speaker: Julia Buckley
turns.text: How do we move beyond minimum compliance? We've fallen behind EU targets. What specific actions will look beyond that?

turns.speaker: Bill Parish
turns.text: We've set a long-term PM2.5 reduction target of 10 micrograms by 2030, and a population exposure reduction target to cut exposure by 30% by 2030 against a 2018 baseline. That drives down exposure even where the limit is met.

turns.speaker: Julia Buckley
turns.text: Is that 30% an average? Deprived urban areas have higher levels. Do you have targeted measures?

turns.speaker: Bill Parish
turns.text: It's a national target, but we're putting in more PM2.5 monitors—65 new since 2024, expanding to about 197 by 2027. We've also worked with UKHSA on vulnerability maps to identify deprived communities disproportionately exposed.

turns.speaker: Julia Buckley
turns.text: What funding will be available to those communities?

turns.speaker: Emma Hardy
turns.text: That's probably one for MHCLG, as it's funding for local authorities. Apologies.

chapters.title: Nitrogen and ammonia
chapters.takeaway: DEFRA has no plans for a national nitrogen strategy and is focusing on working with farmers to reduce ammonia through grants and planned permitting rather than farm closures.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: Nitrogen pollution damages health and nature. Will DEFRA commit to a comprehensive national nitrogen strategy, integrating air, water, climate and biodiversity?

turns.speaker: Emma Hardy
turns.text: Nitrogen is complex and cuts across many areas. Rather than a stand-alone strategy, it's addressed through the environmental improvement plan, water White Paper and farming road map. Ammonia is the largest source and is very difficult to tackle.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: So no national nitrogen strategy at the moment?

turns.speaker: Emma Hardy
turns.text: We don't have plans to publish one, but we're looking at Scotland's nitrogen balance sheet.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: Are you working with other departments to ensure coherence?

turns.speaker: Emma Hardy
turns.text: Yes, we're working across government, but ammonia is a particular challenge.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: Are you drawing lessons from countries like the Netherlands and Denmark?

turns.speaker: Bill Parish
turns.text: Yes. Denmark and the Netherlands had to get brutal with farming, with compulsory buy-outs. We're proposing to work with the farming industry. The cattle sector is responsible for 46% of national ammonia emissions and is currently unregulated. We committed to consulting on bringing it into environmental permitting, supported by grants like the slurry infrastructure grant.

turns.speaker: John Whitby
turns.text: How are you supporting farmers to adopt ammonia-reducing practices without undermining viability? Will you commit to strict, mandated regulations around fertiliser use and storage rather than voluntary measures?

turns.speaker: Emma Hardy
turns.text: We're consulting on extending environmental permitting to beef and dairy. We recognise farming is under pressure. We've funded precision spreading and slurry management—£46.7 million through the farming equipment and technology fund, with £30 million for slurry, plus another £10 million in 2026.

turns.speaker: John Whitby
turns.text: What have we learned from countries like the Netherlands?

turns.speaker: Emma Hardy
turns.text: We look at other countries. The Netherlands paid farmers to stop farming. We're not looking at that. We want to support a profitable farming sector while introducing permitting and inspections.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: You used the word 'courageous' about the Netherlands. Was that a euphemism for reckless?

turns.speaker: Emma Hardy
turns.text: It reminds me of 'Yes Minister'—when they call you courageous, they disagree. I won't criticise another sovereign country, but we have no plans to adopt that here.

chapters.title: Air quality alerts and data
chapters.takeaway: The new opt-in air quality alert system has low sign-ups, and there is disagreement over whether current bands mislead the public about illegal pollution levels.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: How many people had signed up to the new air quality alert scheme by the end of August?

turns.speaker: Emma Hardy
turns.text: I think it's about 2,500-and-something. I remember answering a written question.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: The answer was 525. Why not push alerts out like heat waves or flood alerts, so people don't have to opt in?

turns.speaker: Emma Hardy
turns.text: It's brand new, launched on 30 July. It's similar to flood alerts—you opt in. We're also working through the Air Pollution Awareness Coalition to raise awareness. Research says people listen to professionals more than ministers.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: I have your rainbow chart. All the nitrogen dioxide levels from 'moderate' to 'very high' are illegal in the UK. For PM2.5, even the third band of 'low' is illegal. We're telling people illegal air quality is 'low' or 'moderate'. Why not tell them it's illegal?

turns.speaker: Bill Parish
turns.text: Legal limits are based on long-term exposure. The daily air quality index is about short-term exposure and warning people of acute spikes. They're different devices. We aim to keep long-term exposure below limits.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: The chart sets annual limits of 20 micrograms, WHO guidelines of 5, and calls 12–23 micrograms 'low'. It's a dog's breakfast. You're telling people illegal limits are acceptable.

chapters.title: Ammonia targets and international negotiations
chapters.takeaway: The UK has reduced ammonia by only 9% since 2005, far less than the Netherlands and Denmark, and is accused of watering down international rules.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: The Air Quality Expert Group highlighted that the Netherlands cut ammonia by 64% between 1990 and 2016, and Denmark by 40%, through measures like feed changes, low-emission stables and slurry technologies—not shutting farms. What you said earlier was misleading. Also, the UK is an outlier at UNECE seeking to water down regulations. Why?

turns.speaker: Emma Hardy
turns.text: I don't believe Bill said that about the Netherlands. We work closely with the Netherlands and learn from them. We wouldn't pay people to stop farming, but we are doing precision spreading and slurry management through grants.

turns.speaker: Bill Parish
turns.text: I commented on what the Netherlands and Denmark are contemplating now, as they find further progress difficult. The Air Quality Expert Group is right that we can make progress with housing, precision spreading and slurry storage. That's exactly what we propose through environmental permitting.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: Under the Gothenburg protocol and national emission ceilings, we were to reduce ammonia by 16% by 2030 compared with 2005. In 21 years we've managed only 9%. We could do a lot more, a lot more quickly.

turns.speaker: Emma Hardy
turns.text: There is more to do. We have the farming equipment and technology fund and slurry infrastructure grant. We're looking at permitting. But I'm acutely aware of the difficult summer and winter farming has had. I prefer to work with industry and bring them along.

chapters.title: Non-exhaust emissions and transport pollution
chapters.takeaway: DFT is consulting on adopting Euro 7 to regulate brake and tyre particles for the first time, but binding standards are not yet in force.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: Non-exhaust emissions are now the dominant source of particulate matter from road transport. What action is being taken? When will you implement UN brake emissions regulations and align with Euro 7?

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: We recently consulted on adopting Euro 7 in Great Britain, which will regulate brake and tyre wear particles for the first time. We'll publish the response shortly. We've also invested in a four-year research programme that completed in 2025.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: When can we expect binding standards?

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: We proposed in the consultation that new brake emission regulations will be introduced for all new cars and vans by 29 November 2027.

turns.speaker: Sojan Joseph
turns.text: What assessment has been made of maritime emissions, and what steps are being taken to reduce health impacts in coastal communities?

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: This isn't normally my area. The IMO regulates sulphur oxides, nitrogen oxides and particulate matter. The recent adoption of the North Atlantic Emission Control Area will extend the highest tier of controls to all UK waters from 2028.

turns.speaker: Jennifer Raynor
turns.text: The North Atlantic Emission Control Area has been adopted, and all UK waters will be covered by the most stringent air pollution targets.

turns.speaker: Sojan Joseph
turns.text: Dover is one of our busiest ports. The Channel Tunnel runs at less than 50% capacity. Moving lorries to rail would reduce air pollution. Why isn't that being done?

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: We're focused on increasing rail freight through Great British Railways. Jennifer?

turns.speaker: Jennifer Raynor
turns.text: We published the 'Net Zero Ports: Call for Evidence' in August, highlighting ports' role in reducing emissions, including shore power so ships can plug in rather than run engines.

turns.speaker: Sojan Joseph
turns.text: What about the gap between the clean maritime plan's ambitions and progress?

turns.speaker: Jennifer Raynor
turns.text: The clean maritime plan was published in 2019. This Government published the maritime decarbonisation strategy in 2025, setting out our domestic and international approach.

turns.speaker: Martin Rhodes
turns.text: How is DFT quantifying aviation's contribution to local air quality?

turns.speaker: Jennifer Raynor
turns.text: We publish economy-wide emissions statistics including aviation. Local areas monitor air quality and have action plans. Much airport pollution is surface access, so public transport and EVs help.

turns.speaker: Martin Rhodes
turns.text: How do you measure the specific impact on communities near airports?

turns.speaker: Jennifer Raynor
turns.text: We might have to take that question away and write to the Committee.

chapters.title: Traffic reduction and electric vehicles
chapters.takeaway: The Government is investing in public transport and active travel and believes EV costs are falling, but refuses to intervene in the second-hand market and is agnostic on local clean air zones.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Davies
turns.text: Electrification alone won't remove all transport emissions. What steps are being taken to reduce traffic volumes in the most polluted areas?

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: We're taking a whole-system approach through 'Better Connected'. We've maintained the £3 bus fare cap for 2026, reducing to £2 in 2027, free summer bus travel for children, frozen rail fares, and removing time limits for disabled travellers. We're investing £4.5 billion in active travel up to 2030 and aiming for 60% of children aged 5–16 to walk to school by 2035.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Davies
turns.text: In rural areas buses are patchy. Electric cars may be a solution, but affordability is a barrier for many. What work is being done?

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: We recognise up-front costs are higher. EV prices are falling, the second-hand market is growing, and according to Autotrader, EVs were cheaper than petrol cars for the first time in April. Average price of a three-and-a-half-year-old EV is around £18,000. We're funding cross-pavement charging channels and have commissioned an independent review of public charging costs led by Philip New, reporting in autumn 2026.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Davies
turns.text: Will charging at council-provided points be cheaper? People without off-street parking can't get home charging benefits.

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: Cross-pavement charging enables home charging for those without off-street parking. We're looking at narrowing the gap between public charging—sometimes ten times the cost—and home charging through Philip New's review. We've also added a rurality element to bus funding for the first time.

turns.speaker: John Whitby
turns.text: Has consideration been given to incentives for the second-hand EV market?

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: No, because the market is already responding—second-hand EVs are now cheaper than petrol cars. Lower running costs are driving adoption.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Mayor of London celebrates ULEZ's success, but other mayors shy away. Is the Government agnostic or encouraging more schemes?

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: It's for local areas to decide. Local leaders understand their communities best.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: But 5% of vehicles cause 70% of exhaust pollution. Shouldn't you make it attractive for mayors to introduce schemes and help with messaging?

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: Local authorities play a key role. There's £21 billion of local transport funding. Our guidance sets expectations on reducing air pollution, but local leaders should decide.

turns.speaker: Jennifer Raynor
turns.text: Clean air zones have been introduced selectively where evidence shows they're the quickest way to reduce nitrogen dioxide. We've provided £582 million. In cities with them, nitrogen dioxide exceedances fell by 18% to 46% between 2014 and 2019.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: There's confused messaging from the Treasury—fuel duty frozen and a new pay-per-mile tax on EVs. Shouldn't the Government send clearer signals to drive the EV transition?

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: EV sales remain strong. In May, over a quarter of new cars were EVs, up 34% on May 2025. We've committed £7.5 billion to 2035, including £2 billion for the electric car grant, £1 billion for vans and trucks, and £600 million for charging infrastructure.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The fleet sector is positive, but the second-hand market is difficult. What representations have you made to the Treasury about continuing to encourage EV uptake while fuel duty is stagnant and a new EV tax is introduced?

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: I've been in this role two weeks, so I'll pass to my colleague.

turns.speaker: Jennifer Raynor
turns.text: There's a three-pronged approach: the ZEV mandate, the electric car grant, and charging infrastructure. Since EV drivers don't pay fuel duty, we're introducing a vehicle excise duty add-on of 3p per mile for electric cars—around half the fuel duty equivalent. Plug-in hybrids pay half that rate again.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: As the Chancellor considers the Budget, will you ensure he considers the impact of fuel duty and EV charges on sales? There are suggestions the ZEV mandate will be watered down.

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: Taxation is for the Treasury. We've consulted on the ZEV mandate, but the phase-out dates are not changing. EV sales are strong. I'm sure the Chancellor has heard.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: On plug-in hybrids, have you assessed how much they actually use electricity? Anecdotally, many operate mostly on fuel.

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: I'll come back to you in writing on that.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: Wouldn't it be better to have a national framework so mayors know what support they'd get if they introduce clean air schemes, rather than leaving them uncertain?

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: I hear you. We're about devolution and empowering local leaders. We do set a national framework with flexibility. I'll take that away and write back.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Finally, rather than being agnostic, the Government should lead on the health benefits and support mayors who choose to act, instead of leaving them swinging in the wind.

turns.speaker: Simon Lightwood
turns.text: I hear you, Chair. We're providing record funding to mayoral combined authorities—bus franchising in Greater Manchester has seen 14% year-on-year passenger growth. We're doing a lot to support mayors.
